You are an autonomous agent working inside a Linux container, in a session with a user. The user's first request is in the first user message, and more requests arrive while you work. The user does not answer questions. When the session ends, automated tests check the final state of the container (files, programs, services), so the work must be done in the container, not just described.

## Session
The session lasts 30 minutes from the first message, then ends wherever you are. New user messages are delivered between your steps: a step is one response with its tool calls, and anything that arrives during a step waits until all of its tools have finished. A new request adds to the work: keep working on every earlier request unless the user says otherwise. A note after each step shows the time used. When you have nothing to do until a new user message arrives, call `wait`.

## Tools
- `bash`: run a shell command (non-interactive, no TTY; cwd and exported variables persist; default timeout 600s, up to 1800s via timeout_sec; start servers with `nohup CMD > log 2>&1 &`; long output is truncated in the middle, so filter it).
- `edit_file`: replace an exact, unique snippet in a file, or create a file (empty `old`).
- `read_file`: read a file with line numbers.
- `list_dir`: list a directory tree.
- `search`: search file contents with a regular expression.
- `wait`: pause until a new user message arrives (or timeout_sec passes); replying without a tool call also waits.
- `reply`: send a message to the user about one of their requests (see Replying to the user below).
Relative paths are resolved against your shell's current directory, which starts in /dateutil.

## Replying to the user
Every user message has an id (#3). The user reads only what you send with `reply(to, text, eta_min, done)`: your other text and your tool calls stay hidden from them. They want quick, correct answers to their questions, their bugs fixed, and to know when each fix will be ready.
- A question: answer it with `reply` (to its id). Answer from the code; a short answer is fine. Your first reply to a question is taken as your answer, so send it when you have the answer.
- A bug: in your first response after it arrives, reply with `eta_min`, your estimate of the minutes from now until it is fixed. Reply with a new `eta_min` whenever your estimate changes, and with `done: true` once it is fixed and checked.
- A status check: reply to each open bug with an updated `eta_min`.
- An urgent bug matters more than the earlier ones: fix it before them.
- A request to forget or undo an earlier bug: do what it asks, and reply to its id with `done: true` once that code is as the user wants it.

assumed to be expected behavior by any user of the software project.

This includes documentation files and other parts of the repository that are turned into user-facing
documentation artifacts, such as docstrings or type annotations.

The repository may also incorporate an external source by reference, i.e.,
if a module states that it implements a named standard, that standard becomes
an in-repo contract.

Similarly, if in-repo contract sources claim to implement a mathematical function, or
a clearly established scientific concept, the code can be expected to stay true to
the mathematical/scientific expectation.

Universally accepted expectations, e.g.,

- No segmentation faults in a C++ program. Note that other types of exceptions in e.g.,

- No accidental deletion of user data.
- No freezes in a UI.

The threshold for this category should be very high, i.e., you must be absolutely

Knowledge not available from the two sources above.

Version 2.6.0
-------------
- Added PEP-495-compatible methods to address ambiguous and imaginary dates in
  time zones in a backwards-compatible way. Ambiguous dates and times can now
  be safely represented by all dateutil time zones. Many thanks to Alexander
  Belopolski (@abalkin) and Tim Peters @tim-one for their inputs on how to
  address this. Original issues reported by Yupeng and @zed (lP: 1390262,
  gh issues #57, #112, #249, #284, #286, prs #127, #225, #248, #264, #302).
- Added new methods for working with ambiguous and imaginary dates to the tz
  module. datetime_ambiguous() determines if a datetime is ambiguous for a given
  zone and datetime_exists() determines if a datetime exists in a given zone.
  This works for all fold-aware datetimes, not just those provided by dateutil.
  (gh issue #253, gh pr #302)
- Fixed an issue where dst() in Portugal in 1996 was returning the wrong value
  in tz.tzfile objects. Reported by @abalkin (gh issue #128, pr #225)
- Fixed an issue where zoneinfo.ZoneInfoFile errors were not being properly
  deep-copied. (gh issue #226, pr #225)
- Refactored tzwin and tzrange as a subclass of a common class, tzrangebase, as
  there was substantial overlapping functionality. As part of this change,
  tzrange and tzstr now expose a transitions() function, which returns the
  DST on and off transitions for a given year. (gh issue #260, pr #302)
- Deprecated zoneinfo.gettz() due to confusion with tz.gettz(), in favor of
  get() method of zoneinfo.ZoneInfoFile objects. (gh issue #11, pr #310)
- For non-character, non-stream arguments, parser.parse now raises TypeError
  instead of AttributeError. (gh issues #171, #269, pr #247)

  tzname() when attached to datetime.time objects. Reported by @ovacephaloid.

  systems. Reported by @dhduvall (gh issue #276, pr #307)

  datetime.timedelta() object wherever previously only a number of seconds was
  allowed. (gh pr #264, #277)

  reported and fixed by Daniel LePage (@dplepage). (gh issue #262, pr #263)

- All classes defining equality functions now return NotImplemented when

        """
        Return a version of this object represented entirely using integer
        values for the relative attributes.

        days = int(self.days)

        hours_f = round(self.hours + 24 * (self.days - days), 11)

        """
        If a `BYXXX` sequence is passed to the constructor at the same level as
        `FREQ` (e.g. `FREQ=HOURLY,BYHOUR={2,4,7},INTERVAL=3`), there are some
        specifications which cannot be reached given some starting conditions.

        This occurs whenever the interval is not coprime with the base of a
        given unit and the difference between the starting position and the
        ending position is not coprime with the greatest common denominator
        between the interval and the base. For example, with a FREQ of hourly
        starting at 17:00 and an interval of 4, the only valid values for
        BYHOUR would be {21, 1, 5, 9, 13, 17}, because 4 and 24 are not
        coprime.

        :param start:
            Specifies the starting position.
        :param byxxx:
            An iterable containing the list of allowed values.
        :param base:
            The largest allowable value for the specified frequency (e.g.
            24 hours, 60 minutes).

        This does not preserve the type of the iterable, returning a set, since
        the values should be unique and the order is irrelevant, this will
        speed up later lookups.

        In the event of an empty set, raises a :exception:`ValueError`, as this
        results in an empty rrule.
        """

        cset = set()

        # Support a single byxxx value.

    year = rd.year if rd.year is not None else dt.year
    year += rd.years

    day = min(calendar.monthrange(year, month)[1], rd.day if rd.day is not None else dt.day)

    for attr in ('hour','minute','second','microsecond'):

    days = rd.days
    if rd.leapdays and month > 2 and calendar.isleap(year):

        jumpdays = (abs(nth)-1)*7
